title: AI oversight is a cognitive-load risk: 14% of workers using AI report “brain fry”
summary:
A Harvard Business Review article reports findings from a survey of 1,488 full-time U.S. workers (by BCG). Among respondents using AI at work, 14% said they had experienced “AI brain fry”: mental fatigue caused by AI use or oversight exceeding their cognitive capacity. High AI oversight was associated with 14% more mental effort, 12% more mental fatigue, and 19% more information overload. Respondents reporting brain fry also had higher error-frequency scores and more active intent to leave.

The effects depend on how AI is used: applying it to reduce repetitive work was associated with 15% lower burnout scores. For software firms, the emerging risk is that agentic tools shift the bottleneck from producing work to supervising, checking, and coordinating it.
sampleSize: 1,488 full-time U.S. workers across industries and functions
sponsor: Boston Consulting Group — the study is BCG research; all six authors are BCG-affiliated
whyItMatters: **Attention can become the bottleneck** — as engineers supervise more AI tools and agents, reviewing and coordinating their output may replace code production as the limiting factor.
**Usage volume misreads adoption** — more AI activity does not necessarily mean better outcomes, while brain fry is associated with higher error-frequency scores and greater intent to leave.
**How AI is used shapes the outcome** — removing repetitive work is associated with lower burnout, whereas intensive oversight and added workload are associated with greater mental fatigue.
recommendedActions: **Measure the load** — add cognitive load, information overload, decision fatigue and AI-related error frequency to engineering pulse surveys.
**Set spans of control** — define reasonable limits for how many AI tools or agents one engineer supervises simultaneously.
**Change the adoption metric** — judge the rollout on quality and business outcomes, not on tokens, generated code or frequency of use.
**Decide where the time goes** — state explicitly whether AI-generated time savings reduce workload or are absorbed by additional work.
risksAndCaveats: **Association, not causation** — the survey is cross-sectional and self-reported, so it cannot show that AI oversight causes the fatigue it tracks.
**Not a software-engineering sample** — respondents span many U.S. industries and functions, although engineering is listed among the functions with higher reported prevalence.

**Different percentages measure different things** — figures such as 12% more fatigue and 15% lower burnout describe survey-score differences, while 14% brain fry and the quit-intent figures describe respondent shares.
